summary: This memo describes an RTP payload format for MIDI, the musical instrument command language. It encodes all commands that can appear on a MIDI 1.0 DIN cable and suits both interactive uses like network performance and streaming. It includes tools for recovering from packet loss. It was replaced by RFC 6295.

eli5.summary: Electronic instruments send notes as little messages. This explains how to put those messages in internet packets so musicians in different places can play together. It was later replaced by RFC 6295.

questions: how does rtp midi recover from packet loss
what is the recovery journal in rtp midi
subtitle: How to carry MIDI music commands in RTP packets, with a built-in way to heal from lost packets.

tldr.problem: MIDI is a fragile command language: one lost command, such as a NoteOff, can leave a note sounding forever. Internet packets get lost, and MIDI had no standard way to ride on RTP and IETF session tools.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries a MIDI command section (timestamped commands) and, over unreliable transport, a recovery journal that summarizes recent stream state so a receiver can repair damage after a loss without retransmission.
tldr.outcome: The format works for live network musical performance and for streaming, and is configured through SDP parameters. This memo was later obsoleted by RFC 6295.

today: RFC 4695 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6295, which is the current specification of the RTP MIDI payload format. Its companion implementation guide is RFC 4696.

sections.title: Why MIDI Needs an RTP Payload Format
sections.content:
The MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) command language is used on stage and in the studio to remote-control instruments, and on web pages as a low-bandwidth substitute for audio streaming. The premise of RFC 4695 is that if MIDI performances could be sent as RTP streams managed by IETF session tools, the MIDI and IETF worlds could combine.

Two uses motivate the work: network musical performance, where musicians in different places play together as if in one room, and content streaming, where MIDI serves as low-bitrate audio coding. The format encodes all commands that may legally appear on a MIDI 1.0 DIN cable, and may be used over unicast and multicast UDP and TCP.

The memo defines the syntax and meaning of the payload, but not the algorithms for sending and receiving packets. A companion document, RFC 4696, gives informative guidance on those algorithms. The format also serves as a mode of the mpeg4-generic format from RFC 3640, to support MPEG 4 Audio Object Types.
sections.eli5: Musicians in different cities could play together if their instruments' messages travelled over the internet. This RFC is the rulebook for packing those messages into internet packages.

sections.title: RTP Packets Carrying MIDI
sections.content:
Each RTP MIDI packet has two parts: the standard RTP header and the MIDI payload. The payload starts with the MIDI command section and may be followed by a journal section. The RTP sequence number starts at a random value and goes up by one (modulo 2^16) for every packet, whatever the transport.

The RTP timestamp sets a base time for the packet, and command times in the payload are relative to it. Its units come from the clock rate set at session setup, not from the packet. For audio rendering the clock rate SHOULD be an audio sample rate of 32 KHz or higher. For example, at 44100 Hz two packets 2 seconds apart differ by 88200 in their timestamps.

One RTP MIDI stream carries one MIDI name space: 16 voice channels plus system commands. Several streams may share one RTP session, each with its own SSRC. Streams that split one name space across several streams MUST use different RTP sessions and the same SSRC and starting timestamp, so a receiver can interleave their commands correctly.

Over UDP, a sender SHOULD NOT create packets larger than the network MTU. Whether a journal is present depends on transport: unreliable transport such as UDP defaults to the recovery journal, reliable transport such as TCP defaults to none. If a stream uses the recovery journal, every payload MUST include a journal section.
sections.eli5: Every packet is a small envelope. Inside is a list of music messages and, when the mail might get lost, a recap note of what happened recently.

sections.title: The MIDI Command Section
sections.content:
The command section begins with a header of flags and a length. The B flag chooses the header size: if B is 0 the header is one octet and LEN is 4 bits (a MIDI list of up to 15 octets); if B is 1 the header is two octets and LEN is 12 bits (up to 4095 octets). The J bit says whether a journal section follows, Z says whether the first command has a delta time, and P is the phantom bit for running status.

The MIDI list that follows is a series of delta times and commands. Commands are in the binary format of MIDI 1.0. The first channel command MUST include a status octet; later ones MAY use running status. Standard MIDI File meta-events MUST NOT appear. A System Real-time command embedded inside another command on a DIN cable must be pulled out and coded as its own command.

System Exclusive (SysEx) commands can be sent verbatim (0xF0 ... 0xF7) or split into segments, which lets each data octet get its own delta time and lets large commands span packets. A sender may cancel a segmented SysEx in progress, so it need not buffer a whole command before sending. Unpaired 0xF7 octets MUST NOT appear in the MIDI list.
sections.eli5: Each packet holds a to-do list for the instrument: play this note, change that sound. A little header up front says how long the list is.

sections.title: Timestamps and Delta Times
sections.content:
Each command gets a time through compact delta times, a modified form of the MIDI File format using 1 to 4 octets for a 32-bit unsigned value. The timestamp of command K is the RTP timestamp plus the decoded delta times 0 through K (modulo 2^32), so only the gaps are stored. All command timestamps in a packet MUST be less than or equal to the RTP timestamp of the next packet.

A delta time may be coded in several ways: zero can be written as 0x00, 0x8000, 0x808000 or 0x80808000. A packet can also mark a stretch of time as void of commands by ending its MIDI list with a delta time and no command.

What a timestamp means is chosen with the tsmode parameter. The default comex (command execution) says the timestamp is when the command runs, which suits Standard MIDI Files and new controllers. It is a poor fit for a MIDI 1.0 DIN cable, which takes 320 microseconds per MIDI byte and carries no timestamps, so the RFC adds async (each octet is stamped on arrival) and buffer (a buffer is checked periodically and commands take that moment's time).
sections.eli5: Instead of writing the clock time for every note, the packet says how long to wait after the previous one, like saying 'then two beats later'.

sections.title: The Recovery Journal
sections.content:
A lost MIDI command can cause a transient artifact (one note fails to play) or an indefinite artifact (a lost NoteOff leaves a note sustaining, or a lost Channel Volume change makes a whole channel too loud or soft). The recovery journal mandate is that a performance rendered from a stream over unreliable transport MUST NOT contain indefinite artifacts. The system does not retransmit packets.

Instead, every packet includes a journal describing the stream's history back to a checkpoint packet. When a receiver sees a gap, it compares its own history with the journal in the packet that ends the loss and executes MIDI commands to repair the difference, turning indefinite artifacts into transient ones. A receiver MUST treat the first packet it receives as one that ends a loss event.

The journal has three levels: a 3-octet header with a 16-bit checkpoint sequence number, optional system and channel journals, and per-command-type chapters. Chapters include Program Change (P), Control Change (C), Note On/Off (N) and Pitch Wheel (W) on channels, and system chapters for commands such as Active Sense and System Exclusive.

Which packet is the checkpoint is set by a sending policy, chosen with j_update. The default closed-loop policy uses receiver feedback (such as RTCP reports) to keep the journal as small as possible. The anchor policy always uses the first packet and needs no feedback but gives larger journals. The open-loop policy sets no rule for the sender and relies on the session description to protect commands receivers cannot repair.
sections.eli5: It is like a friend who whispers a quick recap in every message: 'remember, the volume is up and the C note is still on.' If you missed a message, the recap puts you right.

sections.title: Session Setup with SDP
sections.content:
RTP does not manage sessions, so RTP MIDI relies on tools such as SIP and RTSP, which describe streams with SDP. The media type rtp-midi marks a native stream, and the clock rate is given on the rtpmap line; the memo sets no default. A "minimal" stream with no parameters uses the recovery journal over unreliable transport, comex timestamps, and leaves the rendering method unspecified.

A second kind, mpeg4-generic in mode rtp-midi, uses an MPEG 4 Audio Object Type (General MIDI, Wavetable Synthesis or Main Synthetic) to turn MIDI into audio. One RTP MIDI access unit maps to exactly one packet.

Parameters customize streams. They cover stream subsetting (cm_unused, cm_used), journal behavior (j_sec, j_update, ch_default, ch_never, ch_anchor), timestamps (tsmode, octpos, mperiod, linerate), packet duration (rtp_ptime, rtp_maxptime, guardtime), stream labelling (musicport) and rendering. rtp_ptime and rtp_maxptime replace SDP's ptime and maxptime, which MUST NOT be used, because a 0 ms media time is essential for some uses but forbidden by the offer/answer model. The guardtime parameter caps the gap between packets.

Appendix C also gives interoperability rules for RTSP content streaming and for SIP network musical performance, where parties MUST support unicast UDP and General MIDI sessions.
sections.eli5: Before playing together, the two sides swap a settings sheet saying how fast the clock ticks, which messages they will send, and what sound machine to use.

sections.title: Extensibility
sections.content:
The format deliberately covers only the commands that can legally appear on a MIDI 1.0 DIN cable. It does not carry Standard MIDI File meta-event or metric timing data, and it has no transport tools for user-defined commands apart from System Exclusive. By design there is no general extension mechanism; new payload formats are encouraged for specialized musical uses.

A few extension points exist. New token values for j_sec and j_update can define new journal formats and sending policies in standards-track documents. New MIDI renderers can be added through the rendering parameters. If future versions of MIDI define the four reserved System commands (0xF4, 0xF5, 0xF9, 0xFD), standards-track documents may add resiliency support for them.
sections.eli5: The rulebook only covers what a classic MIDI cable could carry. Anything fancier is meant to get its own new rulebook.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Security
sections.content:
RTP congestion control requirements from RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 apply. In applications such as network musical performance the packet rate follows the gestures of a human performer, so senders MUST watch the MIDI source for patterns that cause excessive packet rates and reduce the packet rate when transcoding.

Authentication of incoming RTP and RTCP packets is RECOMMENDED, for example with SRTP (RFC 3711). Without it, attackers could forge MIDI commands into a stream, damaging speakers and eardrums, or craft packets to exploit client bugs. Session management SHOULD authenticate session descriptions, since they can carry initialization data, and URLs in the url and smf_url parameters SHOULD use HTTPS (RFC 2818).

The rule that lets split streams share an SSRC value and starting timestamp weakens the usual randomization of those values, which the memo notes reduces one RTP security aspect.
sections.eli5: Anyone who could slip fake notes into the stream could blast a loud noise into your speakers, so the sender should prove who it is.

fields.name: B
fields.desc: 0 means a one-octet header; 1 means two octets.

fields.name: J
fields.desc: 1 means a journal section follows the command section.

fields.name: Z
fields.desc: 1 means the first command is preceded by a delta time.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Phantom bit: 1 if the first channel command's status octet was absent in the source stream.

fields.name: LEN
fields.desc: Octets in the MIDI list; 4 bits gives up to 15.

items.label: Head 0xF0, tail 0xF0
items.desc: Opens a segmented System Exclusive command.

items.label: Head 0xF7, tail 0xF0
items.desc: A segment in the middle of the command.

items.label: Head 0xF7, tail 0xF4
items.desc: Empty sublist that cancels a segmented command in progress; may follow first or middle, never last.

children.note: 3 octets, includes checkpoint packet sequence number
